The Hong Kong Observatory said a broad trough of low pressure over the northern part of the South China Sea off the Guangdong coast is developing into an area of low pressure. As the associated convective cloud clusters are currently concentrated to the south, more time is needed for consolidation, and a judgment on whether it will develop into a tropical depression can only be made when it approaches the Guangdong coast. The Observatory pointed out that if the area of low pressure develops into a tropical depression, it will assess whether the No. 1 Standby Signal needs to be issued before 6 a.m. on Tuesday (July 15).

The Observatory also noted that, according to current forecasts, the low-pressure system will be closest to Hong Kong early tomorrow morning, passing within 100 kilometres of the territory. Heavy showers, thunderstorms and squalls are forecast for tomorrow (July 15), and the Rainstorm Warning Signal or the Localised Heavy Rain Advisory may need to be issued. Strong winds will blow offshore, and some low-lying areas may experience flooding. On Wednesday (July 16), rain will be heavy at times at first, and strong offshore winds will persist.

The Observatory forecasts that this year's typhoon season in Hong Kong will last from June to October. The first No. 1 Standby Signal of the year was issued on July 2, when Severe Tropical Storm Yinxing over the South China Sea approached the territory and brought more than 30 millimetres of rainfall to many parts of Hong Kong the following day. Yinxing passed about 600 kilometres to the southwest of Hong Kong.
